description: We are a team of researchers committed to change, seeking to develop innovative solutions with significant social impact. Our skills include programming, animation, research, and writing. We are looking for expertise in interface design and visual communication.
summary: Our project tackles three critical challenges in space education for children aged 7–12: translating complex Martian survival science into an intuitive format, teaching real engineering trade-offs rather than isolated mini-games, and grounding play in authentic space agency data. Our solution is KHIPU MARS, a browser-based, single-player Mars habitat mission simulator set at the Tambo Alfa outpost near Jezero Crater. The strategic advantage is turning abstract planetary telemetry into tangible systems thinking. Instead of artificial arcade points, players take on one of four CHAPEA-inspired astronaut roles—Mission Commander, Flight Engineer, Medical Officer, or Science Officer—to survive a 28-sol emergency before an ESA resupply capsule arrives. At the core of the interface is the Khipu Mission Ledger, inspired by the Andean khipu, featuring four vertical resource cords with five knots each (representing 20% reserve increments) and predictive "ghost knots" to preview consequences before committing. Powered by open NASA datasets (MEDA, MRO, DONKI, RAD, ECLSS, JPL Horizons) and terrestrial Mars-analogue soil research from La Joya, Peru (CIP), every decision triggers cascading reactions across life support, solar power, crop growth, radiation shielding, and delayed Earth communications (Chaski Relay), empowering young learners to think like real planetary engineers.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

KHIPU MARS is a browser-based, single-player Mars habitat mission simulator designed for children aged 7–12. Set at the Tambo Alfa outpost near Jezero Crater, players step into a 28-sol survival scenario after a dust storm damages their landing cargo, requiring them to maintain habitat operations until an orbiting ESA resupply capsule arrives.

  • Role Selection: Players choose one of four CHAPEA-inspired roles (Mission Commander, Flight Engineer, Medical Officer, or Science Officer), each unlocking specialized investigation actions and diagnostic readouts while the remaining crew operates collaboratively.
  • Four-Stage Sol Cycle: Each Martian day progresses through four stages: Solar Report (environmental status), Decision (selecting operational responses), Reveal (calculating system consequences), and Close the Sol. Critical emergencies introduce real-time countdown timers (3 to 5 minutes) to create tactical urgency.
  • The Khipu Mission Ledger: Instead of complex spreadsheets, players interact with an interface inspired by the Andean khipu. It features four vertical resource cords (Water/Supplies, Oxygen/Food, Power, and Radiation Alert Level). Each cord has five knots, where each knot represents a 20% resource reserve. Before committing to a choice, players use predictive "ghost knots" to preview how adjusting one resource triggers cascading trade-offs across life support, power, La Joya soil-based crops, radiation shielding, and delayed Earth communications (Chaski Relay).

What benefits does it have?

  • Teaches Systems Thinking: Replaces isolated mini-games with interconnected cause-and-effect mechanics, showing children how conserving water increases energy demand or how seeking radiation shelter pauses external science.
  • Data Integrity & Scientific Literacy: Integrates real NASA datasets (MEDA, MRO, DONKI, RAD, ECLSS, JPL Horizons) and International Potato Center (CIP) Mars-analogue soil research from La Joya, Peru, while transparently distinguishing measured observations from simulated engineering outputs.
  • Cognitive Accessibility: Visualizes percentages and telemetry through illuminated knots and color-coded states, eliminating arbitrary arcade points and helping children aged 7–12 grasp complex engineering trade-offs at a glance.

What is the intended impact of the project?

  • Inspiring Future Planetary Engineers: Equips young learners with practical intuition about closed-loop life support, space weather hazards, and resource autonomy.
  • Scalable STEM Classroom Tool: Designed as an accessible, zero-installation web application that teachers, science museums, and outreach programs worldwide can easily integrate into elementary and middle school STEM curricula.
  • Cultural Representation in Space Exploration: Demonstrates that Indigenous knowledge systems and South American scientific research play a meaningful, functional role in modern aerospace design and education.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

  • Frontend & Web Development: Built using standard web technologies (HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript) to ensure lightweight, cross-platform browser compatibility without requiring high-end hardware.
  • Data Processing & Mathematical Modeling: Used Python (with scientific libraries for data parsing and regression) to process NASA open datasets and calibrate deterministic simulation formulas for solar dust attenuation ($\tau$), ECLSS water mass balance, radiation dose accumulation, and Earth–Mars radio latency.
  • Design & Prototyping: UI/UX wireframes, Andean khipu vector assets, character illustrations, and habitat schematics were created using digital vector and graphic design tools, alongside AI-assisted voiceover synthesis for the pitch presentation.

How is your project creative?

  • Functional Andean UI Metaphor: Rather than using the khipu merely as visual decoration, we translated the historical Inca knot-recording system into a live, interactive telemetry dashboard where knot illumination directly encodes 20% resource incrementsand system ripple effects.
  • Peruvian Aerospace Identity: Connects local heritage and science to Mars exploration—naming the base Tambo Alfa (after Inca waystations), naming the delayed communication system Chaski Relay (after Inca messengers), and incorporating real Peruvian soil analogue research from La Joya, Arequipa.
  • Narrative Debrief ("Your Khipu"): Replaces traditional "Game Over" or numerical high-score screens with a personalized visual record of the knots tied during the 28 sols, allowing players to review the exact history of their decisions.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Age-Appropriate Cognitive Load (Ages 7–12): Introduced mechanics progressively across four narrative acts, paired clear text with visual knot indicators, and capped emergency timers at 3–5 minutes to balance excitement without causing frustration.
  • Scientific Honesty: Explicitly separated real NASA measurements (e.g., Curiosity RAD data from Gale Crater or Perseverance MEDA data from Jezero) from game-level engineering assumptions so players learn accurate scientific boundaries.
  • Hackathon Scoping & Accessibility: Prioritized a single-player, browser-based architecture with automated crew mates and deterministic state logic to guarantee a polished, playable, and bug-free demo within a 48-hour development window.
